posts.author: MichaelH
posts.content_md:
Something strange happened on the way to making a two-channel hologram yesterday...

I made a master hologram of a sand-dollar yesterday morning which came out nice and bright and clean and Susan suggested a two-channel, front and back of the same subject. Being in the groove I set about doing just that.

I exposed the left half of the plate, put the plate in my drying box while flipping the subject, got the plate back out and switched the mask so that the left half of the plate was covered and the right clear. Exposed, developed and found that the right channel was bright and clear and the left look dim and ugly. Examining the final bleached hologram lead me to believe that the plate had moved during the first exposure, mostly because I couldn't find any other cause.

So I set about trying again. Because I already had the second channel subject set up, I exposed this plate "backwards" right to left (for anyone who missed it, the first plate was exposed left to right).

After processing the left channel was again dim and ugly with the right being bright and clear. What the?

Looking at this second plate it almost looks like the left channel was under-exposed. Which is odd because all my exposures are automated and both channels were exposed the same amount of time.

I can't find any sources of stray light and don't believe object movement is at fault since I would expect the second channel in the first hologram to be dim rather than the first (since I had just flipped the subject).

Anyone have any ideas? I'm going to try a third time today and will post the results when I have them. At the moment I'm out of theories.

posts.author: MichaelH
posts.content_md:
Well, this has gone behond the realm of concidence an on to alien influenced madness.

Just kidding about that last part.

I shot another two-channel last night with the same results. In this case I didn't bleach the hologram before finding out how it went and found that again, the left channel was dim and ugly. It also appeared to have received more light than the right channel.

I've checked the light ratios between the channels and both are spot on at 3:1 and the exposure times were correct for each channel.

The only theory I have at the moment is perhaps murphy was visiting me and somehow the shutter didn't close fast enough on the left channel (three times in a row, right) which caused it to be over-exposed. I've done a series of tests on the shutter and software controlling it and it's worked properly in each test, so this isn't much of a theory.

I'm going to be doing another this morning with a different subject and will also post the results.

posts.author: jeff-blyth
posts.content_md:
> **MichaelH:** Colin Kaminski wrote:And you remembered to unblock all object beams?I just re-checked the holograms and on the channel that's dim, the subject is clearly lit by the object beam (there was only one) rather than just the backlighting provided by reference spillover.

It does sound suspiciously like a polarized light problem to me.

An experiment I would try is to stick an "L" shape made of Scotch tape

onto a glass plate. Then to see if either bars of the L brighten things up at all when interposed in one of the beams.

The reasoning is that Scotch tape or at least "Cellux" brand tape has a circular polarizing effect. (Strictly speaking not perfectly circular but elliptically polarizing). 

Jeff

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
It just dawned on me why I could always see the reference beam mirror in a tranmission hologram when I am really close to the hologram, I mean really close (of course you need the coherence length). 

A hologram is made from two sets of waves. The reference wave and the modulated obect wave. When this is recorded into a transmisison hologram and illuminated, parts of the illumination beam that match the object wave will replay the reference wave. So if your eyes are really close to the plate, you will find a small part of the object modulation that reconstructs the reference beam and any other potential beams or reflections to the plate. This may not make sense the way I am putting and I am sorry for that but when I make transmisison holograms and I get real close to the plate I can see my H1 reference mirror (it sure has more scratches and dust then I thought). YOu can see every single defect on it (not to mention the rest of my table where blockers were missing).

Again be careful not to let the laser enter right in your eye, even thought your eye is close to the plate, the plate is rotated in such a way that no laser light enters your eye directly. 

I just never thought about why I was able to see the reference wave through a figurine modulated object wave.

posts.content_md: The reason that you see the scratches, etc., on your reference mirror upon replay of a transmission holo is that you made a Gabor type hologram of those features. You should be seeing "conjugate twins" of the defects when looking back at the source.
